jyotiṣmatī
(‘Full of light’)
------------------------------------------
The Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) describes several methods to attain calmness and steadiness of मिन्द्. (vide 1.33-39). One of them is to meditate on the suṣumnānāḍī. This results in a knowledge of the चित्त or one’s मिन्द्. This knowledge, being full of सत्त्व, is compared to a jyoti or light (jyotiṣmatī = full of light). As a result, the योगि is able to transcend all sorrows.

Jyotiṣṭoma
(‘praise of light’)
------------------------------------------
Of the several types of वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्, the ज्योतिष्टोम is also one, belonging to the सोम group. Its standard form is the अग्निष्टोम.
Stoma (= praise) is a form of chanting the stotras (Ṛgvedic chants) in which the verses are increased by repetition to a certain number. So, a स्तोम is known by a number. For example: trivṛt-स्तोम (three fold or nine).
In the ज्योतिष्टोम sacrifice, the four stomas that are chanted are: trivṛt, pañcadaśa, saptadaśa and ekaviṁśa. These are called four jyotis or lights. Hence the name ज्योतिष्टोम.
See also AGNIṢṬOMA.

Jyotir Maṭha
------------------------------------------
With a view to consolidating and continuing his work of rejuvenation of Vedāntic religion, शङ्कर (A.

-820) established four Maṭhas or monasteries, in the four cardinal directions of the country. The one he established in the north is known as ज्योतिर् मठ or Uttarāmnāya मठ. Toṭakācārya (one of the four chief disciples of शङ्कर) was its first abbot.
The place where this मठ is situated is called Jośīmaṭh. It is 32 kms. (20 miles) below and away from the well-known Himālayan place of पिल्ग्रिमगे, बदरीनाथ or Badarī. It is at a height of 1800 meters (6100 ft.).
Since it is impossible to stay at Badarī during winter, the chief priest (known as ‘Rāval’) of the नारायण temple shifts to ज्योतिर् मठ along with the उत्सवमूर्ति (procession-image) and other essential articles, generally in November. He shifts back sometime during May.
There is an ancient temple of नरसिṁह here. There is also a temple of शिव (known as Jyotīśvara). A cave where शङ्कर used to sit in meditation and a mulberry tree under which he used to worship are also located here.
See also DAŚANĀMĪ.

Jyotirliṅgas
(‘liṅgas of light’)
------------------------------------------
When ब्रह्मा and विष्णु were quarrelling about their mutual greatness, शिव is said to have manifested himself as a jyotirliṅga or लिङ्ग (pillar) of light. He told them that, between them, whoever succeeded in finding his (liṅga’s) extremity, was the greater one.
Twelve liṅgas, spread all over India, are specially designated as ज्योतिर्लिङ्गस्. पिल्ग्रिमगे to these is considered as very meritorious.
These ज्योतिर्लिङ्गस् are: Somanātha (in Gujarat), Mallikārjuna (in Śrīśaila, Andhra Pradesh), महाकाल (in उज्जयिनी, Madhya Pradesh), परमेश्वर or ओङ्कारेश्वर (in ओङ्कार, an island in the नर्मदा river), Kedāra (in the हिमालयस्), Bhīmāśaṅkara (at the source of the river Bhīmā in Maharashtra), Viśveśvara (in काशी or वाराणसी, Uttar Pradesh), त्र्यम्बकेश्वर (near नासिक् in Maharashtra), वैद्यनाथ (in Citābhūmi, Bihar), Nāgeśa (in द्वारका, Gujarat), Rāmeśvara (in Setubandha, Tamil Nadu) and Ghṛṣṇeśa (in Śivālaya, near Daulata-bad of Maharashtra).
The Śivapurāṇa (Koṭirudrasaṁhitā) narrates the legends connected with these liṅgas.
